brief.notification_title: AI rout deepens: Nasdaq futs -1.5%, BTC below $62k
brief.market_summary: Anthropic's record IPO did not stop the selloff. The S&P 500 fell 2.02% to 7,175.83 for its sixth straight loss, Asian chip markets dropped about 5%, and Nasdaq-100 futures are down another 1.5% pre-market with VIX at 29.93. Treasuries are the main beneficiary: the 10Y is about 4.99% pre-market (CNBC), down from 5.05% at Thursday's close, even though the Fed is still on course to hike in December. Brent fell 3% to $89.20 as Gulf exports recover and US inventories build. Crypto fell with tech: BTC is at $61,646 after a record $541m outflow from IBIT.
brief.since_last: Yesterday's headline was "Anthropic lifts futures", and that support has gone. ANT priced at $83, opened at $111.50, closed at $97 and trades at 89.21 pre-market. Thursday's data pointed to slower growth with hot prices. Philly Fed came in at 6.3 against 20.6 expected, while its prices-paid index rose to 58.2, the highest since June 2022. Continuing claims rose to 1.763m against 1.710m expected, the Leading Index fell 0.3%, and existing home sales hit their lowest since 2010. The Fed is still hawkish: Paulson wants more hikes (n23, n177), and CME prices about 95% odds of 25bp in December. Even so, the 10Y has fallen about 6bp to roughly 4.99% as investors buy safety. Gold is at a 14-month low and the dollar index, at 103.88, is at its highest since April 2025. Brent dropped about $2.80 from Thursday's $91.98 settle. Spot crypto ETFs lost $714m in a day. Data caveat: the calendar stamps the claims, Philly Fed, Leading Index, KC Fed and TIPS-auction releases on 20 Nov, but the research notes and yesterday's brief place them on Thursday 19 Nov, so I treat them as Thursday releases.

economic_data.takeaway: This is a large miss and the lowest reading since May. New orders were -0.4 and the capex index halved to 18.9. Prices paid jumped to 58.2, the highest since June 2022. Growth is slowing while input prices rise, which is the worst mix for equities because the Fed can't ease. It helps 7-10Y Treasuries on growth fears but keeps the front end anchored to hikes.

Initial claims are still low, but continuing claims rose 70K, so people who lose jobs are taking longer to find new ones. This is a gradual softening, not a break, and on its own it won't stop a December hike.
Adds to the growth-scare case behind the duration rally. GDPNow was cut to 3.2% from 3.4%, so current growth is still solid.
A strong beat that contradicts Philly. The regional surveys are mixed, which is one reason I'm not reading Philly as a recession signal.

economic_data.release: Housing: starts / permits / pending / existing sales
economic_data.takeaway: Mortgage rates are back up to 7.35% (MBA), and permits and sales are falling. Existing home sales are at their lowest since Aug 2010. Housing is where the Fed's hikes are biting first, which supports the slower-growth side of the duration case.
The real yield is about 25bp above the last auction. High real yields set a high hurdle for gold, BTC and long-duration tech, which links all three selloffs.

Builds came in well above forecast for both crude and gasoline, a second straight large crude build. With Gulf flows normalising, this is bearish for Brent. Cushing fell 1.2M, which slightly offsets it for WTI.

The headline number matters less than 1-year inflation expectations, last at 4.3%. A reading at or below 4.3% triggers the second IEF tranche. Higher would back up Waller's 50bp argument and could cut the bond rally short.

economic_data.release: PCE / core PCE, Q3 GDP (2nd), durable goods
economic_data.takeaway: This is the last major inflation print before the December FOMC and comes in a holiday-thinned week. A hot core PCE would revive 50bp talk; CME currently prices about 5% odds of 50bp.

sections.summary: The S&P 500 fell 2.02% Thursday to 7,175.83, its sixth straight loss, and the Dow closed below 50,000 for the first time since June. Futures are lower again, with NQ -1.51% and ES -0.66%, led by chips and software. Strong earnings from NVDA, WMT and KEYS are being sold, and that tells you this is a de-rating driven by rates and positioning.
key_points: Week: S&P -5.49%, Nasdaq -5.86%, SMH -10.81% (-19.6% over a month). VIX is 29.93, +55% on the week.
Pre-market: INTU -9.7%, AMD -7.0%, INTC -5.2%, NVDA -2.4% (lowest in over a year), ANT 89.21 vs $97 close and $83 IPO price. AAPL is +0.5% on agentic-AI hiring (n27).
Even defensives fell Thursday (XLP -1.45%, XLU -1.24%), but they are still positive over a month (+3.16% and +2.40%).
Credit is holding up: HYG is -0.58% on the week against the S&P's -5.5%. That points to an equity unwind, not funding stress.

sections.summary: Treasuries are heading for a fifth straight weekly gain as investors seek safety. The 10Y is about 4.99% pre-market (CNBC), down from 5.052% at Thursday's close, and the 2Y is around 4.71%. Bills tell a different story: they keep repricing higher for a December hike, and Fed speakers (Paulson, Waller) remain hawkish. Intermediate bonds are working, the front end is pinned and HY is softening slightly.
key_points: Par curve, Thursday: 2Y 4.76%, 10Y 5.04%, 30Y 5.40%; 2s10s +28bp. The 10Y TIPS auction cleared at 2.903% real, up from 2.653%.
Bills: 4-week auction 4.050% (prior 3.955%), 8-week 4.110%, 13-week 4.147%. The funds target is 3.75–4.00% with about 95% odds of 25bp in December.
Foreign buying of T-bonds slowed to $80.8bn from $108.6bn (TIC), and the FT notes oil no longer drives bonds while inflation concerns persist (n144). That is a reason to prefer IEF over TLT.
LQD is flat on the week and HYG -0.58%. Citi says long-duration bonds are the trade if sentiment worsens further (n9).

sections.summary: Brent is $89.20, -3.0% from Thursday's $91.98 settle, on track for a third weekly loss (week-ago settle $95.84) and -21% over a month. Supply is normalising: Gulf and Hormuz flows are near pre-war levels, Iran is preparing to restart exports, and US inventories built well above expectations. The geopolitical spikes overnight (a Houthi strike on Riyadh, tanker mines) were sold.
key_points: EIA: crude +3.38M vs +0.40M expected, gasoline +5.19M vs +1.70M, Cushing -1.21M. WTI is $82.30.
Supply: OPEC's October output rose 1.97mbpd (n21), and Iran is moving to restart exports despite the US blockade (n80).
Upside risks: Trump weighing an Iran decision (n50), Iran refusing inspections (n18), about one tanker incident a day (UOB). UBS calls the selloff overdone (n32).
BNO's 58.84 close (+1.41%) came before the overnight drop, so expect it to open lower. OPEC+ sets 2027 policy on Sun 29 Nov.

brief.instructor_take: Strip away the Anthropic noise and the key fact this week is that the market is selling good news. NVDA guided $130bn against a $125bn consensus, Walmart raised its guidance and Keysight posted record revenue, and all three were sold. When good news stops lifting prices, what you're watching is valuations coming down, not earnings breaking. The cause is the discount rate: a Fed hiking from 3.75–4.00%, a 10Y near 5% and a 10Y TIPS auction at 2.90% real. That one real-yield story connects gold (-7.8% on the week), BTC (-10.9%) and SMH (-10.8%). Thursday's data made it worse rather than better. Philly Fed fell to 6.3 while its prices-paid index hit a four-year high, so the Fed gets slowing growth without relief on inflation and has no reason to come to the rescue. A less experienced investor might miss the other side of this: HYG is only -0.6% on the week, so credit isn't confirming a crisis. A six-session losing streak with VIX near 30 also tends to end in a sharp rebound (n51). That's why I'm not selling everything here, and also why I'm not trying to catch the bottom. My positioning is heavy in T-bills, adding to intermediate Treasuries only on preset triggers, no new semis or crypto, and letting HPE, Dell and Wednesday's PCE show whether good news starts working again. The swing factor today is the UMich 1-year inflation-expectations number at 10:00. I'd be wrong if it comes in hot and Waller gets more support for 50bp, because then bonds stop being the hedge and cash is the only safe place.

top_ideas.title: T-bills stay the core while the Fed hikes
top_ideas.one_liner: Bills pay ~4.1% and reprice up with each hike; keep cash here
top_ideas.thesis: With a December hike about 95% priced, bill yields are rising: the 4-week auction cleared at 4.050% vs 3.955% and the 13-week is 4.147%. SGOV earns that with almost no price risk. It is also the source of cash for the IEF trigger and any later semis rebuild, so it does two jobs.
top_ideas.reasoning: I start with what pays me to wait. The funds target is 3.75–4.00%, the market expects a 25bp hike in December, and the 4-week auction already clears at 4.05%. Each hike gets passed into SGOV within weeks because the bills roll over so quickly. Meanwhile stocks, gold, crypto and even staples all fell Thursday, so 'diversified' exposure isn't diversifying right now, and cash is the one asset that cannot fall in price. A less experienced investor sees cash as a missed opportunity. I see it as an option: it lets me buy IEF on today's trigger or SMH on a confirmed turn without having to sell something at a bad price. I'd change my mind if the 13-week yield fell below 4.0%, or if Fed speakers signalled the hiking cycle ends in December. Either would mean locking in duration instead. Neither is happening: Paulson wants more hikes and Waller wants 50bp.

top_ideas.entry: Keep the existing position and add idle cash at market today. Leave this sleeve as the funding source for the IEF second tranche and any later SMH rebuild.

top_ideas.sizing: Keep about 20–30% of the portfolio in this sleeve while VIX is near 30

top_ideas.title: IEF second half only on today's UMich trigger
top_ideas.one_liner: Add 2nd IEF half only if UMich 1-yr inflation exp. ≤4.3%
top_ideas.thesis: Slower growth (Philly 6.3, Leading Index -0.3%, housing at a 16-year low, continuing claims 1.763m) and investors seeking safety are pulling the 10Y back toward 4.99%. That favours intermediate Treasuries even while the Fed hikes. Inflation is the risk, so the second tranche depends on 1-year inflation expectations staying at or below 4.3%.
top_ideas.reasoning: My first-half IEF was bought around 90.67 and closed Thursday at 90.82. It is working modestly, and it fell less than any other holding on a -2% equity day, which is the job I bought it for. The 5.20–5.25% price trigger is moving further away as yields fall, so today's event trigger matters. If UMich 1-year expectations print at or below 4.3%, the market can keep pricing slower growth without fearing an inflation spiral, and IEF's roughly 7-year duration gains about 0.7% for every 10bp fall in yields. I use IEF rather than TLT because the 30Y at 5.40% carries more term-premium and supply risk: foreign T-bond buying slowed to $80.8bn from $108.6bn, and inflation worries are keeping long-end yields high (n144). The trap for a student is Philly's prices-paid index at 58.2. This is not a clean disinflationary growth scare, so I won't add on soft growth headlines alone. If expectations come in above 4.3%, I keep the first half and go back to waiting for 5.20–5.25%. A 10Y close above 5.30% means I was wrong about duration.

top_ideas.title: Still no semis until good news gets rewarded
top_ideas.one_liner: Semis -10.8% on the week; wait for Dell/HPE reaction before buying
top_ideas.thesis: SMH is at 447.48, -10.8% on the week and -19.6% over a month, after NVDA beat and raised and still fell to a one-year low. Pre-market AMD is -7% and Asian chip benchmarks are about -5%. I keep the avoid through HPE (Mon) and Dell (Tue) and rebuild only on confirmed strength.
top_ideas.reasoning: The avoid has worked: SMH fell another 2.6% Thursday and futures point lower. I keep it because the evidence hasn't changed. When a company guides $130bn against $125bn expected and the stock makes new lows, the problem is the multiple, and high real yields (the TIPS auction at 2.90%) compress the multiples of long-duration growth stocks the most. Anthropic's IPO also pulls AI allocation away from incumbents: ARK alone put $90.8m into ANT. The next real test is next week's AI-hardware reports, especially Dell against a $6.48 estimate. What I'm watching is the reaction, not the beat. If Dell beats and semis rally and hold, that's the first sign good news is working again. A less experienced investor tends to lower the re-entry bar as the price falls. I keep the $500 trigger, roughly last week's level, so that I'm buying after the trend has recovered rather than guessing the bottom. I'd be wrong if a sharp short-covering rally carries SMH back above $500 quickly, in which case I give up some upside and buy in at a higher price.

lesson.concept: Real yields as the hurdle rate
lesson.explanation: A real yield is a Treasury yield minus expected inflation. The cleanest market measure is the TIPS yield. It is the return you get on a risk-free asset after inflation, so every asset that pays nothing now (gold, bitcoin) or pays mostly in the distant future (high-growth tech) has to clear it. When real yields rise, those assets lose value even if nothing about them has changed, because the discount rate applied to their future payoff went up.
lesson.todays_example: This week the 10Y TIPS auction cleared at 2.903% real, up from 2.653%. Over the same week gold fell 7.8% to a 14-month low, BTC fell 10.9% to its lowest since July, and SMH fell 10.8%, even after Nvidia beat and raised. Three different assets fell for one shared reason, which is why diversifying across them hasn't helped. T-bills and intermediate Treasuries have held up.
